source.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
source.authors: George Ma; Zhong-Yuan Liang; Irene Y. Chen; Somayeh Sojoudi

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates SAE features associated with reasoning, not individual neurons or the mixed neuron responses described in the claim. Its results concern a related representational unit, so they do not test any listed version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports experiments on SAE feature activations and interpretations, rather than neuron polysemanticity. I record relevant adjacent SAE-feature results under versions ["none"]. Its steering benchmark results concern downstream performance, not whether a neuron or feature has one coherent meaning, and are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates contrastively selected SAE features (residual-stream dictionary directions) for whether they track reasoning, using token injection and LLM-guided counterexamples. It mentions polysemantic neurons only as background motivation for SAEs and reports no measurement of individual neuron responses, polysemanticity rates, causes or architecture dependence. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that contrastive correlations are not, by themselves, sufficient evidence for monosemantic reasoning SAE features. They attribute this to sparsity favoring low-dimensional cue correlates and recommend causal and adversarial validation. They draw no conclusion about neuron polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The study selects SAE features contrastively and tests them with token injection and LLM-guided false-positive/false-negative construction; it does not use a neuron polysemanticity measurement or the cited original neuron examples.
record.method_sensitivity: Token-injection classifications vary by model, layer, and reasoning dataset; the paper reports between 45% and 90% of candidates in token-driven categories across configurations. For example, Gemma-3-12B-Instruct at layer 22 has 45% on s1K and 56% on General Inquiry CoT, while Gemma-3-4B-Instruct at layer 17 has 90% and 79%, respectively.

fits_no_version.finding: Many contrastively selected 'reasoning' SAE features in LLMs (45%-90% across Gemma-3/DeepSeek configs) respond to injected cue tokens in non-reasoning text. None of the context-dependent features analyzed survived LLM-guided counterexample tests.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features selected by contrast between reasoning and non-reasoning text mostly track lexical or discourse cues, not reasoning itself.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The experiments concern SAE features rather than neurons and the authors scope conclusions to contrastively selected features and studied settings. LLM-guided falsification analyzes sampled context-dependent features (up to 20 per configuration); the paper acknowledges that results do not rule out information distributed across many features or represented nonlinearly. Steering is described as small-scale and supplementary.
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract steering benchmark accuracies (Table 5), token concentration and entropy statistics (Table 11), feature-set overlap (Table 15), or per-example Appendix G cases because these concern SAE feature properties or downstream benchmark behavior, not individual neuron polysemanticity. Alternative feature-ranking metrics in Tables 9–10 repeat the same adjacent SAE-feature question.

untested.parts: No vision models or neurons studied.
No measurement of the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens; only residual-stream SAE features.
The stylized l1/Top-K theory concerns SAE decoding favoring low-dimensional cues, not superposition causing neuron polysemanticity.
Not addressed; cross-model differences concern SAE feature token sensitivity, not neuron polysemanticity.
Does not reanalyze canonical polysemantic neurons.
Not addressed for neurons; the finding that feature interpretations depend on falsification tests is about SAE features.

record.verdict_notes: Rows are correctly linked to none. Two inconsistencies in the source: the main text reports 248 context-dependent features analyzed, but Appendix E.5 says 153; Figure 9 gives mean 3.4 while Table 14 gives mean 2.4. Neither affects the gate decision.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test individual neurons in vision models or InceptionV1.
The paper studies SAE features in language models, not the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts.

The stylized analysis concerns sparsity favoring low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional variation; it does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by representing more features than neurons.
The paper does not test neuron polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise without capacity pressure.

It reports SAE-feature results across model/layer settings, not changes in the share of polysemantic neurons caused by activation function, architecture, or regularization, nor the claimed performance tradeoff.
It does not reanalyze canonical polysemantic neurons or the examples in the claim to determine whether their mixed inputs share a feature.
It does not test how neuron polysemanticity classifications vary with activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.note: These are SAE feature results, not neuron results.
